slides.title: Contract Architecture & Advanced Solidity
slides.subtitle: Interfaces  •  Libraries  •  Custom Errors  •  ETH Reception

slides.title: Part 1 — Connecting to Last Lecture
recap_points: Inheritance — one contract extends another using is keyword
Parent & Child contracts — child inherits all parent functions
Constructor Inheritance — parent constructor runs first
Function Overloading — same name, different parameters
Function Overriding — virtual in parent, override in child
Enums — fixed set of allowed values for a variable
slides.transition: Today we take contract architecture one step further. In real blockchain applications, we rarely build everything inside one contract.

slides.title: Real-World Multi-Contract Architecture
slides.statement: A real application can contain dozens of contracts — all communicating with each other.
slides.point: These contracts need to communicate with each other. Today we learn how that communication works.

slides.title: Abstract Contracts
slides.subtitle: Incomplete contracts that define structure for child contracts

slides.title: What is an Abstract Contract?
slides.definition: An abstract contract is a contract that is intentionally incomplete. It is designed to be used as a base for other contracts.

normal_function.label: Normal Function

abstract_function.label: Abstract Function

key_points: Contains at least one function with no body
Cannot be deployed on its own
Child contracts MUST implement all abstract functions
Can also contain fully implemented functions

slides.title: Abstract Contract — Animal / Dog / Cat
slides.label: Animal.sol + Dog.sol + Cat.sol
steps: Deploy Dog → call sleep() → 'Animal is sleeping'

slides.title: Why Abstract Contracts? — Real-World Use
slides.analogy: Every payment system must process a payment — but each system implements it differently.
slides.insight: Define the requirement in the parent. The child provides the actual implementation. This is abstraction.

slides.title: Interfaces
slides.subtitle: The foundation of contract-to-contract communication in Solidity

slides.title: What is an Interface?
slides.definition: An interface defines WHAT functions a contract exposes to the outside world — without any implementation. It is the standard way contracts communicate with each other.
slides.analogy: An interface is like an API specification. It tells you what endpoints exist and what they return — not how they work internally.
rules: Implementing contract must define all functions

slides.title: Abstract Contract vs Interface — Side by Side
slides.summary: Abstract Contract = partial implementation. Interface = pure contract standard.

slides.title: Implementing an Interface
slides.label: ICalculator.sol + Calculator.sol

slides.title: How Contract-to-Contract Communication Works
slides.key_formula: Interface  +  Contract Address  =  Contract Instance  →  Function Call
slides.explanation: Every deployed contract on Ethereum has a unique address (e.g. 0x1234...ABCD). To call its functions, you combine that address with an interface — giving Solidity enough information to make the call.

slides.title: Practical — Calculator + CalculatorUser
slides.label: CalculatorUser.sol

key_line.explanation: The address alone doesn't tell Solidity which functions to call. We cast it to the interface type to create a typed contract instance.

slides.result: Two smart contracts just communicated on-chain.

slides.title: Reading & Modifying Another Contract's State
slides.label: ICounter Interface — Read vs Write

read.label: Reading State
read.detail: view call — no gas cost — returns value immediately

write.label: Changing State
write.detail: state-changing transaction — costs gas — creates a transaction

slides.note: When a state-changing call happens through an interface, gas is consumed. This reinforces the view vs non-view distinction in a cross-contract context.

slides.title: Libraries
slides.subtitle: Reusable utility logic — shared across contracts without inheritance

slides.title: What is a Library?
slides.definition: A library is a collection of reusable functions. Instead of repeating utility logic across contracts, you write it once in a library and use it everywhere.
slides.analogy: A library is like a math toolkit. You don't build a calculator into every room — you have one math library everyone shares.
rules: Functions are internal (same contract) or external (deployed separately)
Called directly: LibraryName.function() or via using for

slides.title: Library — Basic Example & using for
slides.label: MathLibrary.sol + Calculator.sol
slides.key_insight: using MathLibrary for uint attaches all library functions to the uint type. The variable itself becomes the first argument.
steps: Result is identical — syntax is cleaner

slides.title: Practical Library — ArrayUtils
slides.label: ArrayUtils.sol + ArrayExample.sol
steps: Notice: values.max() — max() is called on the array itself
slides.note: using ArrayUtils for uint[] attaches max() to any uint[] array in this contract.

slides.title: Custom Errors
slides.subtitle: Structured, gas-efficient error handling in Solidity

slides.title: Custom Errors — Why & How
slides.definition: Custom errors are named error types defined with the error keyword. They are more gas-efficient than string revert messages and provide structured error information.

require.label: require() — Old way
require.cons: Stores string on-chain — higher gas cost

custom_error.label: Custom Error — New way

slides.title: Custom Errors — Vault Contract
slides.label: Vault.sol
steps: Try withdraw() from a different address → NotOwner error
Try withdraw(amount > balance) → InsufficientBalance error with values

slides.title: constant & immutable
slides.subtitle: Values that never change after being set

slides.title: constant vs immutable
slides.definition_constant: constant — value is fixed at compile time. Must be assigned when declared. Never changes.
slides.definition_immutable: immutable — value is assigned once during contract deployment (constructor). Cannot change after that.

slides.title: receive() & fallback()
slides.subtitle: How Ethereum contracts handle incoming ETH

slides.title: receive() and fallback() — ETH Reception
slides.question: What happens when someone sends ETH directly to a contract address?
slides.receive_def: receive() is called when the contract receives Ether with empty calldata (a plain ETH transfer).
slides.fallback_def: fallback() is called when no matching function is found — or when ETH is sent with data but no receive() exists.
decision_flow: Does calldata match a function signature?

slides.title: Practical — EtherReceiver Contract
slides.label: EtherReceiver.sol

key_variables.name: msg.value
key_variables.meaning: Amount of ETH sent with this call (in wei)

key_variables.name: address(this).balance
key_variables.meaning: Total ETH balance held by this contract

steps: Send test ETH to the contract address
Observe the Received event fires in Remix logs
Call getBalance() → shows ETH balance of the contract

slides.title: Real-World Protocols That Use Interfaces
slides.label: Why Interfaces Matter in Production

real_world.name: ERC20 Token Standard
real_world.detail: IERC20 is an interface. Every token — USDT, LINK, UNI — implements the same interface: transfer(), approve(), balanceOf().

real_world.name: ERC721 NFT Standard
real_world.detail: IERC721 is an interface. Every NFT contract implements ownerOf(), transferFrom(), safeTransferFrom().

real_world.name: Chainlink Price Feeds
real_world.detail: AggregatorV3Interface lets your contract call Chainlink's price feeds without knowing internal implementation.

real_world.name: Uniswap V2 Router
real_world.detail: IUniswapV2Router02 interface lets any contract interact with Uniswap swaps and liquidity pools.

slides.key_insight: Every production protocol interacts with other contracts through interfaces — never through internal implementation knowledge.

slides.description: How all today's concepts fit together in a real Blockchain Application

Pure API — external functions only, no implementation
Unique identifier for every deployed contract
Call another contract using interface + address
Reusable utility functions shared across contracts
Attach library functions to a Solidity type
Structured, gas-efficient error with optional parameters
Value fixed at compile time — never changes
Value set at deployment — fixed forever after
Handles unmatched function calls / ETH with data

slides.title: Thank You
slides.subtitle: Lectures 7 Complete
slides.key_message: Today we moved from writing individual smart contracts to thinking about how smart contracts are designed as systems.
recap: Abstract contracts provide reusable base structure
Interfaces define how other contracts communicate with you
Libraries allow reusable utility logic across contracts
Custom errors provide structured & efficient error handling
constant = compile time  |  immutable = deployment time
receive() handles plain ETH  |  fallback() handles unmatched calls
slides.closing_statement: Ethereum applications are not one contract. They are SYSTEMS of contracts — inheriting, communicating, sharing libraries, and following interface standards. This is the foundation of every DeFi protocol, token system, marketplace, and DAO.
